name: SN65LVDS1DBVR
title: Single-channel LVDS line driver (SN65LVDS1) and receivers (SN65LVDS2, SN65LVDT2)
summary: A family of three single-channel TIA/EIA-644 LVDS parts in SOT-23-5 and SOIC-8. The SN65LVDS1 turns a 5 V tolerant LVTTL input into a 350 mV typical differential output for a 100 Ω line, at up to 630 Mbps. The SN65LVDS2 receiver resolves ±100 mV at up to 400 Mbps, has open-input fail-safe and gives an LVTTL output; the SN65LVDT2 adds a 110 Ω termination across its inputs. All run from 2.4 V to 3.6 V over –40 °C to 85 °C and go high impedance below 1.5 V.
key_figures: |VOD| 350 mV typ, 247 mV to 454 mV (VCC ≥ 3 V) into 100 Ω
driver 1.5 / 1.8 ns typ; receiver 2.6 / 2.5 ns typ

circuits.title: Simplified schematic: SN65LVDS1 to SN65LVDT2 link
circuits.description: A logic output drives the D input of an SN65LVDS1, which sends the bit as a differential pair on Y and Z over a 100 Ω trace to the A and B inputs of an SN65LVDT2. The receiver's built-in termination loads the line, and its R output feeds a logic input. The two ends have their own supplies, VSUPPLY at the driver and VCC at the receiver, and share ground.
notes: LINE_P and LINE_N are a 100 Ω differential trace.

circuits.title: Point-to-point topology
circuits.description: One driver and one receiver joined by a balanced pair of 100 Ω characteristic impedance. A single 100 Ω resistor across IN+ and IN- at the receiver end matches the line. The driver takes a single-ended logic input and the receiver gives back a single-ended output.
notes: LINE_P and LINE_N are a 100 Ω balanced interconnect; R1 sits at the receiver.
Design values: driver and receiver supplies 2.4 to 3.6 V, driver input 0.8 to 5.0 V, signaling rate DC to 400 Mbps, one receiver node, receiver input 0 to VCCR – 0.8 V, ground shift ±1 V.

circuits.title: Recommended LVDS bypass capacitor layout
circuits.description: Two ceramic capacitors in parallel from the 3.3 V supply to ground: 0.1 µF for the middle frequencies and 0.001 µF, the value worked out from the supply-current step, rise time and noise budget. The smaller one goes closest to the chip.

circuits.title: Multidrop topology
circuits.description: One driver at the start of a shared 100 Ω pair, receivers tapped onto the pair along its length on short stubs, and a last receiver at the far end with a resistor of about 100 Ω across the pair. Only the far end is terminated. Up to 32 receivers may share the bus.
notes: Stubs from the bus to U2 and U3 are kept as short as possible.

Design values: driver and receiver supplies 2.4 to 3.6 V, driver input 0.8 to 5.0 V, signaling rate DC to 400 Mbps, 100 Ω line and termination, 2 to 32 receiver nodes, receiver input 0 to VCCR – 0.8 V, ground shift ±1 V.

circuits.title: Driver test circuit for common-mode output voltage
circuits.description: Measures the driver's common-mode output. Y and Z each go through a 49.9 Ω, 1 % resistor to a shared node; 50 pF from that node to ground, and VOC is read there. VOC(SS) is the settled level and VOC(PP) the peak-to-peak disturbance at each input edge, with the input switching between 1 V and 1.4 V.
notes: Generator: edges (tr, tf) ≤ 1 ns, repetition rate 0.5 Mpps, pulse width 500 ± 10 ns. CL includes the probe and jig capacitance lying within 0.06 mm of the part. VOC(PP) is read on equipment with at least 300 MHz –3 dB bandwidth.

circuits.title: Receiver input threshold (VIT+, VIT–) test circuit
circuits.description: Sets a small differential input on top of a common-mode voltage. A pulse generator with 100 Ω across it feeds A and B through two 1000 Ω resistors; a second 100 Ω sits across A and B, and a source VIC lifts the generator's low side above ground. Each input has 10 pF to ground and the R output 15 pF. The differential input steps to just past a threshold (+100 mV or –100 mV) to show the output switching.

parts.note: left out when an SN65LVDT2 is tested

notes: Input signal: 3 Mpps, 167 ns long, transitions under 1 ns.
V1 pin 1 is its positive side.

circuits.title: Driver test circuit for differential output timing
circuits.description: Loads the driver with 100 Ω, 1 % across Y and Z and 10 pF from each output to ground. Delays run from the input crossing 1.4 V (VCC = 3.3 V) or 1.2 V (VCC = 2.7 V) to the differential output crossing 0 V; rise and fall times are taken between 20 % and 80 % of the output swing. The input swings 0.8 V to 2 V.
notes: Generator: edges (tr, tf) ≤ 1 ns, repetition rate 50 Mpps, pulse width 10 ± 0.2 ns. CL includes the probe and jig capacitance lying within 0.06 mm of the part.

circuits.title: Receiver timing test circuit
circuits.description: Drives A and B with complementary signals between 1 V and 1.4 V, so the differential input swings ±0.4 V, and loads R with 10 pF. Delays run from the differential input crossing 0 V to the output crossing 0.45 VCC; rise and fall times are taken between 20 % and 80 %.
notes: Generator: edges (tr, tf) ≤ 1 ns, repetition rate 50 Mpps, pulse width 10 ± 0.2 ns. CL includes the probe and jig capacitance lying within 0.06 m of the part.

operation.text: Three single-channel LVDS parts to TIA/EIA-644: the SN65LVDS1 line driver, the SN65LVDS2 line receiver, and the SN65LVDT2, which is the SN65LVDS2 with a line-termination resistor built in. Each comes in a 5-pin SOT-23 and an 8-pin SOIC. Drivers are rated for signaling rates to 630 Mbps and receivers to 400 Mbps. Signaling rate counts voltage transitions per second, in bps. All run from 2.4 V to 3.6 V over –40 °C to 85 °C.

Typical output 350 mV into 100 Ω, at least 247 mV. Typical propagation delay 1.7 ns for the driver and 2.5 ns for the receiver. Typical power at 200 MHz: 25 mW for the driver and 60 mW for the receiver. Bus-pin ESD above 9 kV. Receiver threshold under 100 mV.

The SN65LVDS1 takes an LVTTL input and drives a differential output at a nominal 340 mV swing about a 1.2 V common mode. It is meant to drive a 100 Ω line, terminated at the far end in a resistance equal to the line's impedance.

The SN65LVDS2 turns an LVDS input into an LVTTL output. It resolves inputs of ±100 mV. Since an LVDS driver sits at 1.2 V common mode, it still reads the line correctly with 1 V of ground difference between driver and receiver.

The SN65LVDT2's internal resistor replaces the separate termination at the end of the line. It suits a point-to-point link, or the last receiver of a multidrop bus; fitting it at every node would load the bus, alter its impedance and cause reflections.
The SN65LVDS1 meets its specifications from 2.6 V to 3.6 V. Below 1.5 V, or during power-up before 1.5 V is reached, a power-on reset holds the outputs at high impedance.
LVDS requires a driver common-mode output of 1.2 V ± 75 mV. A sensing circuit and control loop in the SN65LVDS1 supply common-mode current to hold the output at that point from 2.6 V to 3.6 V.

The driver input thresholds are the TTL ones, 2.0 V and 0.8 V, shared by 3.3 V and 5 V TTL. The input accepts signals up to 5 V whatever the supply, so 3.3 V and 5 V TTL and CMOS sources can drive it. The decision point is about 1.4 V; with 5 V TTL or CMOS signals that fixed, ground-referenced threshold produces some duty-cycle distortion, which depends on the input slew rate and the data rate and matters at high speed or where duty cycle is critical.
NC pins have no connection to the die. Grounding them on the board improves heat removal.

The D input is a CMOS inverter behind 50 Ω with a 7 V Zener for ESD and a 300 kΩ pulldown to ground; left open, the input reads low and the outputs go low (Y low, Z high). Each output half has a 7 V Zener for ESD and switches nominally 3.5 mA current sources into the load, through 5 Ω, with 10 kΩ in the stage; to first order the output behaves as a constant-current source.

Between –100 mV and 100 mV a differential receiver's output is undefined. When the inputs are open (driver at high impedance or cable unplugged), little current flows from the line and 300 kΩ resistors inside pull A and B toward VCC. An AND gate with thresholds near 2.3 V spots both inputs high and forces R high. Only in this case is the output defined with less than 100 mV of input. A termination resistor across A and B keeps fail-safe working; a termination network with a DC path to ground can overcome the pull-ups and defeat it.

The receivers work from 2.6 V to 3.6 V. Their output high level follows the supply: at least 2.4 V (TTL compliant) with VCC above 3 V, and at least 1.9 V with VCC from 2.6 V to 3.0 V. Below 1.5 V, or before 1.5 V is reached at power-up, both inputs and the output go to high impedance.

Valid input runs from ground to 0.8 V below VCC. With a 100 mV minimum differential, common-mode values from 0.05 V to 2.45 V are supported at a 3.3 V supply, and 0.05 V to 1.65 V at 2.5 V. The SN65LVDS2 accepts compliant LVDS inputs with common mode from 0.05 V to 2.35 V, and at 3.3 V the receivers meet their sensitivity from GND to 2.5 V.
The SN65LVDS2 and SN65LVDT2 follow any input that stays within the differential and common-mode limits, not only LVDS signals.

The SN65LVDS2 input stage is a differential pair of high impedance with 300 kΩ from each input to VCC; the SN65LVDT2 adds 110 Ω across the inputs. Each input has a 7 V Zener for ESD. The R output is a CMOS inverter with 5 Ω in series and its own 7 V Zener.

Below 1.5 V the driver outputs, and the receiver inputs and output, are high impedance. From 1.5 V to below 2.4 V behaviour is undefined and nothing is guaranteed. From 2.4 V to 3.6 V is normal operation; some limits hold over the whole range and others depend on the supply voltage.

Differential output is nominally 350 mV across the supply range. At 3.3 V the minimum stays inside the LVDS window of 247 mV to 454 mV; from 2.4 V to 3 V it can fall to 200 mV, which is below the LVDS minimum, so a link run there needs its noise margin checked.

Large board-level capacitors (10 µF to 1000 µF) cover up to the kHz range but their lead inductance makes them poor at digital switching frequencies, so smaller capacitors (nF to µF) go next to the IC. Ceramic chip capacitors in 0603 or 0805 have about 1 nH of lead inductance, against about 5 nH for a leaded part. With a 200 ps rise time, a 1 A current step and 200 mV of allowed noise the local value comes to 0.001 µF; 0.1 µF beside it bridges to the board-level capacitor above 10 µF, and the smallest value sits nearest the chip. The receivers use the same scheme.

Any balanced metal pair that meets the LVDS standard serves: PCB traces, twinax, twisted pair or flat ribbon. Nominal characteristic impedance 100 Ω to 120 Ω, varying by no more than 10 % (90 Ω to 132 Ω).

A microstrip runs on an outer layer over a plane; a stripline runs on an inner layer between two planes. Two lines close together form a coupled pair; driven differentially, the pair's differential impedance is the sum of the two odd-mode impedances and depends on the spacing as well as width and dielectric. With S under 2W the pair is tightly coupled. Keep width and spacing constant along the run and the two lines symmetrical.

The resistive termination converts the driver current to the receiver's input voltage and must match the line within 10 % for incident-wave switching, needed at the highest rates: 90 Ω to 110 Ω for a 100 Ω line. Place it as close to the receiver as possible to keep the stub short; the SN65LVDT2 builds it into the receiver. On a multidrop bus terminate only at the end or ends: SN65LVDS2 receivers on the branches, an SN65LVDT2 only at the bus end.

The receivers read high above 100 mV and low below –100 mV differential and accept up to 600 mV. Outputs meet LVTTL levels with VCC from 3 V to 3.6 V; from 2.4 V to 3 V the high level can be as low as 1.9 V, which the driven logic must accept.

With the driver's 1.2 V common mode and a receiver range from ground to VCC – 0.8 V, a link works with ground difference plus common-mode noise of about ±1 V between ends. LVDS is aimed at chip-to-chip, board-to-board and rack-to-nearby-rack distances; where 1 V is not enough, M-LVDS parts or extended-common-mode LVDS receivers such as the SN65LVDS33 are the alternatives.

One driver, a shared bus and two or more receivers, at most 32. With the driver at one end only the far end needs terminating; moving the driver elsewhere leaves one end open, although a central driver would halve the longest flight time. Every branch makes a stub that should be minimal; added device and stub capacitance lowers the loaded bus impedance and causes reflections at the change. With constant, evenly spread loads the terminations can match the loaded impedance; otherwise reflections must fit in the noise budget.

Each device runs from one supply, 2.4 V to 3.6 V. Driver and receiver may sit on separate boards or equipment with separate supplies; the ground difference between them is expected to stay under 1 V. Use board-level and local bypass capacitance.
Striplines, between two planes, emit and pick up less but the planes add capacitance; TI recommends routing LVDS as microstrip where possible.

FR-4 or similar is usually adequate. If TTL/CMOS edges are faster than 500 ps, a dielectric near εr = 3.4 (Rogers 4350, Nelco N4000-13) suits better. Construction found to work: copper 1/2 oz (15 g) start plated to 1 oz (30 g); exposed circuitry solder-plated 60/40 to at least 7.62 µm (0.0003 in); plated-through holes with at least 25.4 µm (0.001 in) of copper; bare copper under the solder mask, finished by hot-air solder levelling.

Use at least two separate signal layers to cut TTL/CMOS-to-LVDS crosstalk. Four layers: LVDS signals, ground, power, TTL/CMOS signals, with 127 µm (0.005 in) between the ground and power planes so their capacitance bypasses transients. Six layers: LVDS signals, ground, power, ground, ground, TTL signals; each signal layer then has a ground plane between it and power and both outer signal layers reference ground, at higher cost.

Couple the two lines of a pair closely, routed as 100 Ω differential, and match their electrical lengths to limit skew and reflection. Between single-ended traces, and between neighbouring pairs, apply the 3-W rule: edge gap more than twice the trace width, or centre spacing three widths. Avoid sharp 90° bends; use successive 45° turns. Autorouters do not always account for crosstalk and reflections.

A ground plane directly under the traces gives high-frequency return current the shortest loop and the least crosstalk and emission. Keep traces short over unbroken ground; slots and holes in the plane raise return inductance. Short, low-impedance ground pin connections reduce ground bounce.

Connect each power and ground pin to its plane through one or more vias right beside the pin; a power plane near the top shortens the via. Put bypass capacitors close to the VDD pins, at the corners or under the package. Use small parts (0402 or 0201) or X7R surface-mount types, each pad tied to its plane by vias tangent to the pad. A 0402 X7R has about 0.5 nH of body inductance and behaves as an inductor above roughly 30 MHz; parallel values such as 100 pF, 1 nF, 0.03 µF and 0.1 µF extend coverage to a few hundred MHz. Power and ground planes 2 to 3 mils apart make the best bypass: about 500 pF per square inch with 2 mil FR4. Where a ground pad leaves no room, put the capacitor on the back of the board. Keep VDD vias close to the pin but covered by solder mask so solder does not wick into the barrel.

Space single-ended traces and pairs at two to three trace widths; parallel runs shorter than the edge's wavelength couple negligibly, and long parallel runs need more space. Staggering traces on alternate layers allows closer horizontal spacing. Give each signal via an adjacent ground via; a typical via adds about 0.5 pF to 1 pF in FR4. Avoid plane discontinuities under traces, keep traces short and group like functions together to reduce EMI.
IBIS models are available for these devices.
